title: From Oracle's Offices to a Karur Kiosk: Falooda Brand Hits Rs 9 Crore
excerpt: Pradeep Kannan walked away from a Rs 1-lakh-a-month operations role at Oracle in 2019 to open a 10×10-foot falooda kiosk in his hometown. Seven years on, The Falooda Shop has 18+ outlets across India and Dubai and revenue above Rs 9 crore.
body:
• Pradeep Kannan left his Rs 1-lakh-a-month operations role at Oracle in 2019 to open a 10×10-foot falooda kiosk in Karur, Tamil Nadu.
  • His brand, The Falooda Shop, has grown to 18+ outlets across India and Dubai and now earns over Rs 9 crore in revenue.
  • The business runs on a franchise model, with the brand providing staff, raw materials, and training to franchisees.
  • Earlier this month, Kannan announced the brand's first North India outlet, opening soon in Gurugram's Sector 69.

In 2019, Pradeep Kannan walked away from what his social circle called a settled life: a comfortable salary of around Rs 1 lakh a month as Operations Head at Oracle India. He moved back to Karur, a small town in Tamil Nadu, and opened a 10×10-foot kiosk selling falooda. No grand launch, no advertising campaign — just a modest storefront and a plan to turn the classic Indian dessert into what he calls a "modern, premium and franchise-ready concept."

Seven years later, that kiosk has become The Falooda Shop, a dessert-focused quick-service brand with more than 18 outlets across India and Dubai, and revenue exceeding Rs 9 crore, according to NDTV. In a post on X on October 31, 2025, Kannan wrote that people laughed at him for the decision, believing he had "lost it." "Everyone advised me to reconsider," he recalled.

Context & Background

Kannan's path to the kiosk was anything but linear. He graduated from the National Institute of Fashion Technology and began his career in the apparel industry. After earning a management degree from Mumbai, he worked in supply chain management in India and Dubai before joining Oracle, where he rose to operations head. The restlessness that drove him out, he says, was about building something of his own rather than climbing further up a corporate ladder.

The franchise model did the heavy lifting. From the single Karur outlet, the brand expanded to 17 additional stores, including one in Dubai, with franchisees paying an upfront fee while the brand supports them with staff, raw materials, and training. The brand has since widened its menu for millennial and Gen-Z customers, adding items like drinkable faloodas and ready-to-eat falooda in a can.

Kannan's story sits in a familiar Indian pattern of high-flying professionals quitting corporate jobs for food businesses — a trend that has produced brands worth hundreds of crores — but few have started from a literal 10-by-10-foot stall in a tier-3 town.

Impact & Analysis

The Falooda Shop's rise shows how far a standardized franchise system can carry a single-product brand. Falooda, a Mughlai-era dessert of vermicelli, basil seeds, milk, and ice cream, had long been sold mostly by street vendors and small parlours. Packaging it as a premium, franchise-ready concept gave it the consistency needed to scale — the same playbook that built India's big tea and dessert chains. Food franchising remains one of the lowest-barrier entries into entrepreneurship in India, but survival is unforgiving: most new food ventures fail within two years. A brand that crossed seven years and nearly twenty outlets has cleared the hardest filter in the business.

"People laughed at me for leaving my job. I had the perfect 9-5. Operations Head at Oracle India. Good salary. Beautiful family."

— Pradeep Kannan, Founder, The Falooda Shop

Diaspora Angle

The brand's Dubai outlet plants it squarely in the Gulf, home to millions of Indian expatriates and one of the strongest markets for Indian food franchises. For NRIs in the UAE, a falooda kiosk is a taste of home packaged in a modern format — and for entrepreneurial NRIs, Kannan's franchise model is the kind of tested, replicable system many diaspora investors look for when backing ventures back home. His stated ambition to build a "global D2C ice-cream brand" and take The Falooda Shop to "global shelves" points directly at diaspora-heavy markets as the next frontier.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

The immediate milestone is the brand's first North India outlet, taking shape in Gurugram's Sector 69. Kannan announced the move on X on September 9, 2026, writing: "Karur to Delhi NCR. Still processing this one." Entering the Delhi-NCR market — among the most competitive food markets in the country — will test whether a brand built in South India's smaller towns can win over northern consumers.

Beyond that, Kannan says he is building "India's next aspirational D2C ice cream brand in public," suggesting packaged retail is the next leg. His summary of the journey — "small town dreams to AC offices to franchise kitchens to global shelves" — ends, as he put it, with "just the beginning."

"My journey has gone from: small town dreams to AC offices to franchise kitchens to global shelves."

— Pradeep Kannan, Founder, The Falooda Shop
